{{about|the physicist|the politician|Randy Feenstra}}
'''Randall M. Feenstra''' is a Canadian physicist. He completed a bachelor's degree in engineering physics at the [[University of British Columbia]] in 1978, followed by his master's and doctorate in applied physics at the [[California Institute of Technology]].<ref name="eua">{{cite news |title=Carnegie Mellon physicist Randall Feenstra wins 2019 Davisson-Germer Prize |url=https://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2018-10/cmu-cmp102318.php |accessdate=3 June 2020 |work=EurekAlert! |date=23 October 2018|archivedate=3 June 2020|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20200603184309/https://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2018-10/cmu-cmp102318.php}}</ref><ref name="cmuedu">{{cite news |title=Randall Feenstra |url=https://www.cmu.edu/physics/people/faculty/feenstra.html |accessdate=3 June 2020 |publisher=Department of Physics, Carnegie Mellon University|archivedate=3 June 2020|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20200603184309/https://www.cmu.edu/physics/people/faculty/feenstra.html}}</ref> From 1982 to 1995, he was a research staff member at the IBM [[Thomas J. Watson Research Center]] in Yorktown Heights, New York.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Schwarzschild |first1=Bertram |title=Physics Nobel Prize Awarded for Microscopies Old and New |journal=Physics Today |date=1987 |volume=40 |issue=1 |pages=17–21 |doi=10.1063/1.2815291|bibcode=1987PhT....40a..17S }}</ref> Since 1995, he has taught at [[Carnegie Mellon University]],<ref name="eua"/> where he conducts research in semiconductors.<ref>{{cite news |title=Randall Feenstra |url=https://www.cmu.edu/2d-center/faculty/feenstra-randall.html |accessdate=3 June 2020 |publisher=Carnegie Melllon University, 2D Center|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20200603184308/https://www.cmu.edu/2d-center/faculty/feenstra-randall.html|archivedate=3 June 2020}}</ref>

Feenstra is a fellow of the [[American Vacuum Society]], and was the 1989 recipient of its [[Peter Mark Memorial Award]].<ref name="cmuedu"/> He was elected to fellowship of the [[American Physical Society]] in 1997, "[f]or contributions to the development of the Scanning Tunneling Microscope as a spectroscopic tool to probe semiconductor surfaces and surface phenomena,"<ref>{{cite news |title=APS Fellow Archive |url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=F&year=2019&unit_id=&institution= |accessdate=3 June 2020 |publisher=American Physical Society}}</ref> and was awarded the APS [[Davisson–Germer Prize in Atomic or Surface Physics]] in 2019, "[f]or pioneering developments of the techniques and concepts of spectroscopic scanning tunneling microscopy."<ref name="eua"/><ref>{{cite news |title=Davisson-Germer Prize in Atomic or Surface Physics: Recipient Randall Feenstra Carnegie Mellon University |url=https://www.aps.org/units/dcmp/awards/recipient.cfm?first_nm=Randall&last_nm=Feenstra&year=2019 |accessdate=3 June 2020 |publisher=American Physical Society|archivedate=3 June 2020|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20200603184308/https://www.aps.org/units/dcmp/awards/recipient.cfm?first_nm=Randall&last_nm=Feenstra&year=2019}}</ref>
